title: Game Theory (HL) Adventure 2: Prisoner's Dilemma & Dominant Strategies
welcome_lead: Today you'll meet the famous Prisoner's Dilemma and find dominant strategies.
meta_desc: Economics HL Game Theory: prisoner's dilemma, dominant and dominated strategies.
final_note: You solved a prisoner's dilemma by iterated elimination of dominated strategies.

concepts.def: Collusion to restrict output / raise price

walkthroughs.body_html:
Two prisoners, separate cells.

Stay silent (Cooperate) or confess (Defect)? Years in jail:
(C,C)=(1,1); (D,D)=(5,5); (C,D)=(10,0); (D,C)=(0,10).

Defect is dominant for each — yet joint Defect (5,5) is worse than joint Cooperate (1,1). Individual rationality → collective loss.

A strategy is strictly dominant if it gives a higher payoff than any other, whatever the rival does.

It is strictly dominated if another strategy is always better.

Method: iterated elimination of dominated strategies can simplify games to a unique Nash equilibrium.

OPEC members face a prisoner's dilemma. Each gains by cheating quotas — but if all cheat, the price collapses.

Solution attempts: repeated games, audits, monitoring, side payments. Tit-for-tat (Axelrod 1984) can sustain cooperation if the game repeats indefinitely.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a shift in demand and a movement along the demand curve?
options: A movement along the curve is caused by a change in price; a shift of the whole curve is caused by changes in other factors (income, tastes, substitute prices).
Demand always falls when supply increases.
XED measures how often consumers cross-shop between stores.
A change in price shifts the demand curve.

options: Shortage in the market — quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the controlled price, leading to queues, black markets and reduced quality.
